entry.title: Does an Art TV Belong on Your Wall?
entry.summary: And are any of the new models better than The Frame?
entry.content:
Samsung pioneered the idea of the art TV in 2017 with its The Frame: a large-format television you could hide in plain sight as a framed piece of art. And after nine years and 10 generations, the art TV is having a moment, with competition heating up as companies like LG, TCL and even Amazon have released their own versions in the hopes of ending Samsung’s near monopoly in the category.

Each one comes with a flush style mount specially crafted to help the TV sit closer to the wall — and look more like a picture frame. The trade-off, however, is that you won’t be able to adjust it up and down or side to side. I admit to going out of the box, so to speak. I skip the included mount and instead use the Sanus VLL5 mount, which still sits flush to the wall yet allows me to easily hook and unhook the TV without tools (it’s much easier for testing).

As one of the original reviewers of The Frame, I can attest to its near-foolproof ability to fool guests into thinking it was indeed a painting, and that has become even easier as Samsung’s subsequent Frames added a matte screen and access to hundreds of fancy, bespoke frames from DecoTV Frames.

Can any of the newcomers match The Frame’s ability to double as art? Are any of them worth your time and money? I tested them all against the most recent The Frame Pro to see how each one compares as an art TV, concentrating on design and art store offerings, rather than picture quality or tech specs.

Art Store: $5/month or $50/year for access to 5,000 plus works from museum collections; “Streams” Free Tier | Sizes: 55-, 65-, or 75-inches | Smart TV OS: Tizen | Frame options: Modern Brown, Modern Teak, Modern White, or Sand Gold; third party frames available.

The OG art TV, Samsung’s The Frame has had a big head start. Not only has it had time to incorporate feedback from users over the last nine years, but it was also the first to employ a full-time curator. Daria Greene, head of content and curation for the Samsung Art Store, is a former VP of the SCOPE contemporary art fair and consulting curator at Hulu; she and her team license new work to help its art store feel more like a gallery, and less like a digital content library. For me, that means using her curated feeds to find art I may never have looked at before — which adds value to what’s still the best overall art TV experience.

In 2022, Samsung replaced The Frame’s glossy screen with an anti-glare, matte display, and it makes a huge difference for a more realistic look (all the competing art TVs have followed suit with glare-free displays). The Frame also comes with a certification from Pantone that it realistically matches colors as seen under gallery-style lighting. But most importantly, once the TV is in Art Mode, the display uses a built-in sensor to adjust brightness based on ambient light to help artwork look as close to its original as possible. And though Amazon and LG both claim to use the same sensors, Samsung has the most realistic display out of the bunch. For me, this is the biggest difference versus a standard TV, especially in the evening when your surroundings are darker than the screen.

When you purchase The Frame, you can pick one of four different-colored magnetic bezels at additional cost; if you want something specific to match your decor or just a more ornate design, you can choose from the hundreds of frames on DecoTV Frames. The latter are not cheap, but they do lend a much more realistic look when you display your art (and a Black Friday sale is on now if you want to give them a try). I have a thick, brushed gold frame which seriously helps to create the illusion of real art. Samsung also offers a stripped-down version, the standard The Frame (which has wired connections only and a dimmer display), in a wide array of sizes 32 inches to 98 inches; the Frame Pro only comes in 55, 65 and 75-inch sizes.

The Frame Pro also comes with the Wireless One Connect Box. This one piece of hardware houses all its connections and ports, so the only wire that connects to the TV is the power cord. If you want to go for the full framed painting look, you can talk to a professional installer about running cables inside the wall (I live in an older NYC building with masonry walls I can’t drill into, so I bought a cord cover to camouflage mine).

You purchase an art TV for the art, and that’s where Samsung’s long experience with this format shows, with a broader, deeper, and better-organized collection than the competition.

Though I’d like to think I have good taste in art, a collection of over 5000 works can be daunting, so the subscription paired with a Netflix-style interface feels worth the $50 to help me browse and discover new work. (If you don’t subscribe, you only get access to Art Store Streams, Samsung’s free tier that offers 30 pieces of art from the collection every month or lets you display your own photos. You can’t choose your own selections, and each piece will only be displayed for 5 minutes before rotating out.)

I like Samsung’s simple, editorial approach, which features Greene’s curated collections up top, followed by options like museum or gallery, artist, style, period, medium, color, and even mood. You can also upload your own photos to live in the My Art Store section, which also acts as a repository for art you want to save as favorites.

Samsung’s artwork comes from museum partners including MoMA (NYC and San Francisco), Whitney Museum, Art Institute of Chicago, Centre Pompidou, Tate Modern, MFA Boston, Louvre and the British Museum, and offers exclusive art TV access to paintings like Jean-Michel Basquiat’s “Untitled (Two Heads on Gold)” and Keith Haring’s iconic 1982 “Radiant Baby.” Once you scroll the rows of content and decide on a collection, just click to browse the thumbnails of art and click again to preview it on the screen. This month’s curations include MoMA’s collection, along with one spotlighting photographer Cody Cobb and a Happy Thanksgiving slideshow.

Once you’ve chosen your image you can then personalize it. I’m a huge fan of the Manual Art Mode settings, which let you add a mat in different sizes and colors as well as customize the brightness on each piece of art, past what the sensor decides.

Don’t need wireless connection and can live with a little less brightness? The Frame is a little less expensive in the standard version and gives you access to the same art collection.

Art Store: $5/month for access to 5,000 plus works from museum collections; free tier with limited selections | Sizes: 55- or 65-inches | Smart TV OS: LG webOS | Frame options: white or walnut.

In terms of art library scope, the LG Gallery is the closest competitor to Samsung out of the new art TVs, and at $600 for the 55-inch I received, its pricing is also on par with The Frame (the standard version, not the Frame Pro). LG’s Gallery+ store pricing is comparable to the Samsung Art Store, and also offers about the same amount of art. However, LG’s default settings are not as accurate, and the software is a lot clunkier, which makes adjusting anything a lot of work: picture settings are not intuitive, and unless you go through a tedious series of clicks on the remote, it does not offer realistic color and contrast for the actual art. I am a huge fan of LG’s excellent OLED TVs, but was disappointed in the general picture quality of its mini LED display.

LG also touts a matte display and uses an ambient light sensor to adjust the picture. This worked in line with Samsung’s display, but I found problems with the default intensity of the lighting, which tended to overcompensate for my space and gave images an artificial look. LG’s Gallery+ includes Claude Monet’s “Garden at Sainte-Adresse” so I was able to make a direct comparison, and when set next to The Frame, the LG set’s colors were significantly more luminous, showing an almost green ocean and glowing whites. I did the same with Monet’s “Water Lilies” and got the same result. It wasn’t unpleasant to look at and it didn’t have the same screensaver effect as the TCL and the Amazon TVs, it just didn’t look authentic (for what it’s worth, my 20-year-old son actually liked it better). There is plenty of detail, however, and I was impressed with the rendition of the texture of the Monet paintings, which matched The Frame’s display.

The Gallery comes with a white magnetic frame, but if you’d prefer the walnut brown wood color, you can purchase one for an extra $150. The company’s Magic Remote acts more like a pointer, but felt fiddly for me to use, though the TV does come with a stand. It is available in 55-and-65-inches.

Gallery+ is the company’s paid art store and it nearly matches the Samsung Art Store in scope with over 5,000 pieces of art, though instead of a single curator, LG allows its partners to choose what content is included. A free version is included, which lets you choose from a much smaller library of images ranging from fine art like Vasily Kandinsky’s “Pastorale” to photographs of cities, beaches, forests and more to videos of landscapes and animated paintings.

The larger store is organized by categories, with your Recent Views up top, followed by a row of Today’s Recommendations and a gallery called Discover What’s New. Below that, you can choose from specific collections like The Korean Heritage Collection, Warm Thanksgiving Vibes and The Color of Fall. The rest of the store has no particular rhyme or reason but you can search through compilations sorted by museums like The Met and The National Gallery, and modern artists like Martin Parr and Lauren Karp.

Other categories include Sports, Travel, Space and Nature. My favorite was the High-Definition Videos category, which has several iterations of yule logs and bonfires that should come in handy for the winter holidays, as well as scenes like waterfalls at sunset and gorgeous Northern Lights. You can also upload your own images using the LG ThinQ app or through the Photo area in your Gallery+ account. To create a slide show, you can either download the entire collection and hit play, or create your own by adding to My Page and then playing them.

But it’s important to know that LG’s integration of art features into its TV OS needs some work. I am giving them some leeway since this is the company’s first attempt at an art TV, but it does feel something like a work in progress: every time you choose a piece of art to display, you have to navigate through two extra steps compared to other art stores where you click only once. First you click on the thumbnail, then you hit a button to download the content, and then it plays. And then you have to click again to choose whether you want the image in Gallery Mode (which keeps it on the screen when the TV is off) or as a Screensaver (which will turn the image off after a short period of time). Additionally, finding and using the set’s other display settings, like brightness, color temperature and mat (which seems to only allow a grey mat with no other options and then leaves it on for all your other choices unless you go into those specific settings and turn it off) takes so many clicks of the remote, with unclear instructions, that I refused to bother after my first try.

Art Store: Free | Sizes: 55-, or 65-inches | Smart TV OS: Fire TV | Frame options: ten woodgrain, metallic, and painted finishes.

Amazon got into the art TV market this year with the Ember Artline, and I have been pleasantly surprised at how varied and well-organized the more than 2,000 free pieces of art are and how many settings are included to personalize each piece — it’s a substantially heartier collection that budget contender TCL offers, though still severely lacking compared to Samsung’s and LG’s libraries.

The display has a matte finish to deal with glare, and though Amazon insists the Ember Artline does have ambient light sensors, it still struggles to make any of the art look real. Amazon does not include “Garden at Sainte-Adresse” in its catalog, so I chose one of Monet’s “Water Lilies” to compare with The Frame Pro (they didn’t have the same Monets since Samsung has exclusive rights to the works in the MoMA collection). I cannot express how much more like a painting the Samsung looks. Even when I toggled down the brightness and contrast, the Ember ended up looking like a giant screensaver while Samsung could well be a print reproduction.

The Ember Artline does not come with a stand (it is an art TV, after all, and is meant to be hung on the wall), so you will have to plan to get it up on the wall immediately unless you order the legs for $20 extra. It comes with your choice of one of 10 different color magnetic frames, including a deep red Fig, Matte White, Midnight Blue and the Pale Gold I received. You can get extra frames for $75 each.

Amazon touts its curation by Natalia Peschiera, a photo researcher with a background in sourcing images, who leads the curation of Amazon’s Ambient Art Gallery. While it doesn’t stack up to Samsung’s, its mid-sized library of more than 2,000 pieces of art is quite generous, and, you know, free — there’s no paid tier.

The art is sorted into categories such as Modern, Hudson River School and Impressionism, with works like Paul Cézanne’s “Mont Sainte-Victoire with Large Pine,” but you can also browse featured collections like Fine Art, Regional, Motion, Art Movements, Photography, and Film and TV, or by Artist Spotlight, with emerging artists like Joe Horner and Natalie Christensen or a few masters like Degas and Renoir. I was also tickled by regional curations like England and Mexico and the seasonal galleries, among others.

Like TCL, Amazon leans into animated tableaux, with features like Motion Art, Dynamic Art and Interactive Art. And because the settings are not optimized to make the display look like real art, this is an excellent alternative. Here you can find things like koi fish swimming on a blue screen, pristine beaches in French Polynesia, and my favorite fireplace video under Seasonal Motion. Like TCL, it also offers AI Art, which uses Alexa to help you create personalized images by speaking into the remote’s microphone. You can also use Alexa to request a slideshow of a certain collection.

You can only load your own photos through Amazon Photos; if you haven’t used it before, Amazon Prime membership gets you free unlimited full-resolution photo storage, while non-Prime members get 5 GB. Once you set up an account, just link it to the TV, choose the photos you want to display, and the album will automatically show up in your library.

Amazon’s “Match the Room” feature can also be fun to explore. Just scan the QR code on the screen, upload up to 4 photos of your room and it will give you suggestions of personalized art to match your style and decor. I was testing this TV in my son’s room, so the suggestions didn’t quite fit my taste, but it is an interesting feature.

Art Store: Free | Sizes: 55-, 65-, 75 -, or 85-inches | TV Platform: Google TV |Frame options: Off-white and wood-finish frames included; Laredo Factory Frames options available.

TCL is known for offering good value for money, and its new Designer Series art TVs are clearly meant as an affordable luxury alternative, with the bare minimum of bells and whistles. But given the strong competition at the low end of the price scale from Amazon’s Ember Artline, despite its nice design and interesting ambient lighting, the TCL isn’t as compelling an “art TV” as the competition given its limited library and bare-bones presentation of artworks.

The first thing I noticed was that the bezel of the TV is a pleasing, shiny off-white, so you can ostensibly not bother with a different frame if this suits your needs. Great idea, TCL. But if you are interested, a light wood colored frame is included in the box and, as with the bezels that fit The Frame, it simply clicks onto the TV magnetically. Alternative frames are available from Laredo Frame Factory. No stand is included, but you can purchase one separately, and the A300L is available in sizes range from 55 inches to 85 inches.

The TCL has what the brand calls an Ultra-Matte screen that helps control glare to allow the art to look more realistic. However, when compared to the Samsung, its colors did not measure up, and the set does not include sensors to help adjust brightness to the room. I displayed Monet’s “Garden at Sainte-Adresse” on both screens, and the difference in brightness, contrast and saturation was striking. I also noticed that the painting was cut off by about a half-inch on the TCL when compared to The Frame.

TCL only offers a free art store called the Gallery. This includes six categories with 181 pictures in all — though with only 80 pieces of artwork culled from museums and galleries, highlighting artists like Mondrian, Seurat and Monet. Though it is woefully undernourished compared with The Frame, you will get a much larger selection than the free version of the Samsung Art Store. There is also a category called Masterpieces Alive, which animates 13 classic paintings. I guess it could be fun, but for me, seeing the water move and fireworks light up in Van Gogh’s “Starry Night Over the Rhone” was no less than creepy. Art can be displayed as a single piece, or you can highlight your favorites in a collection, then press Play on the remote to create a slideshow, though I couldn’t find an exact scroll rate. Want to display your own pictures? Photos uploaded through the TCL app will live in Ambient Mode.

You can also explore the three other digital modules: AI Art, Relax and Moment. AI Art is exactly what you might think, letting you create your own pictures by mixing words like Dream and Ocean. I still haven’t found one I’d want to save, but it can be engaging. Moment lets you show off personal photos from Google Photos (it uses Google TV OS) to turn your TV into a giant picture frame, and it also offers a folder with seven iterations of a digital clock. Relax is my favorite, with over 20 animated scenes accompanied by matching soundscapes, like a sunset beach or twilight on a lake.

entry.title: I Tried the New BEMT Sunscreens
entry.summary: They’re pretty good, which is a great thing.
entry.content:
Last month, I wrote about the sudden proliferation of sunscreens containing bemotrizinol, or BEMT, a chemical filter that’s been popular abroad for decades and is now FDA-approved. In the time since, I’ve been testing the new batch of sunscreens and went on a lab tour with Cerave (it has a face and body sunscreen launching in December that I’m currently testing) to learn more about the ingredient.

The exciting thing about BEMT is that it’s more photostable than the current UV filters we have, meaning it holds up better than other chemicals when exposed to UV light. It also helps broaden the spectrum of UV protection. Prior to the inclusion of BEMT, sunscreens offered broad spectrum protection, with filters like homosalate and octisalate protecting skin from UVB rays (the rays responsible for sunburn) and avobenzone protecting skin from UVA rays, which impact skin over time. Together, they provide broad spectrum protection, but few filters cover both UVA and UVB light on their own. The main sunscreen filter that does, oxybenzone, has become less popular in recent years due to public concern over absorption into the bloodstream, though the ingredient isn’t deemed unsafe. Still, some consumers prefer not to use it. BEMT is a helpful solve for this. It’s a bigger molecule that doesn’t absorb as readily into skin and protects from similar UV wavelengths. When combined with other filters, BEMT strengthens the formulas we already use by providing added stability, and because it holds up well to light, the filter doesn’t degrade as quickly, offering better protection.

While knowing it offers better protection is great, I was most interested in the way it sits on skin. My favorite formulas, like La Roche-Posay UVAir, are whisper-thin, so I was curious if this new filter would have any noticeable effect on the consistency. To find out, I tested each of the formulas for a week — from a zinc oxide–and–BEMT stick to classic drugstore fare. My general thoughts are that these feel like any other well-made sunscreens, which I’m considering a positive, given that they could’ve gone the way of mineral sunscreens, which in the early days were tough to adapt to despite the benefits. These new formulas don’t feel like a trade-off while offering even better protection from UV light.

I’ve been wearing this one off and on for about a month. It’s the epitome of no-frills. The texture is similar to any other lightweight sunscreen I’ve tried that’s not aiming for a serum or lotion-y texture. It goes on smooth and doesn’t leave a white cast, which makes sense because it’s composed of chemical filters. It’s also a little glowy, but not as much as some of my other sunscreens, which I prefer. It’s not markedly different from the dozens of other formulas I’ve tried, but I’m happy to have it in my rotation.

I’ve also tested the acne-free version, which performs similarly but is just a hair thicker and has a slightly powdery finish. It also feels a bit tackier on the dry down, which could make it a good option if you wear base makeup. Between the two formulas, I would reach for the Ultra Sheer option, which has a lighter feel.

I’m a fan of Ultra Violette sunscreens generally. The Australian brand is known for its lightweight formulas, which feel like skin care. I’ve used other products from the brand and think its formulations are impressive, so I wasn’t shocked that I liked this formula too. It’s a hybrid formula with both chemical and physical filters that’s designed for acne-prone skin and has a slightly matte finish. It also has blurring technology and helps to control oil. I don’t have oily skin and I also have tiny pores, so this wasn’t a noticeable difference, but it did well with my main metric for sunscreens containing zinc — it doesn’t leave a white cast. It’s a bit tinted too, which doesn’t show up on my brown skin tone but might have a slight effect on fairer skin. As for feel: It wears like a moisturizer, and despite having mattifying properties, it doesn’t have a super-powdery feel. It isn’t as slick as some of my other preferred formulas, but I don’t mind the feel. I think this is a good option for anyone wanting to try the ingredient out or is in search of a formula with both zinc oxide and BEMT.

I also tried this stick from Burnd, a hybrid formula that contains both zinc oxide and BEMT. Physical filters can sometimes have a chalky consistency, so I was pleasantly surprised that this went on smoothly. I owe that to the argan oil and vitamin E. It was also remarkably lightweight, and even though it goes on a bit white, it completely disappeared after rubbing it in. It also didn’t leave my skin greasy. The one drawback for me is the scent, which isn’t specific to this sunscreen but zinc oxide more generally. It smells a bit metallic to my nose, which can be annoying to experience throughout the day. Sticks are also tough for me because it can be difficult to apply the appropriate amount of sunscreen — about a shot glass’s worth for the face. I think this works best for reapplication, but I wouldn’t use it as my daily SPF.

entry.title: Your Favorite Advent Calendar Sold Out? DIY One Instead.
entry.summary: I asked creative parents for their tips and learned that making your own is easier than you might think.
entry.content:
If store-bought Advent calendars leave you feeling uninspired, making your own is always an option. And you don’t have to be an experienced crafter or even know how to sew. All you need is a system for arranging 24 or 25 pockets — or gift bags or envelopes — and 24 goodies to fill them. To get you started, I asked creative parents with children between the ages of 2 and 16 for their expert advice on assembling a DIY Advent calendar, including lots of ideas for exactly what to put inside.

“In my experience kids really latch on to holiday traditions, so I always try to keep things low-key enough that they’ll be fun and quick to replicate year after year,” says Erin Boyle, the writer and creative behind Make/Do and a co-author of the book Making Things. Go in with realistic goals so you don’t lose steam before the fun really begins.

Boyle’s family uses a simple cloth-pocket calendar that she designed with her Making Things co-author. “It’s a simple canvas wall pocket — five rows of five pockets each — with a seriously pared-down pattern for even the most novice sewist. I love that I can just pull it out of our small box of Christmas decorations every year and it’s basically ready to go,” she says.

To make one according to Boyle’s pattern, you’ll need cotton duck canvas, a sewing machine and thread, a wooden dowel to give the top structure, and string or cord to hang it. Boyle suggests using mini-clothespins and small squares of paper with numbers written on them as labels for each pocket. But you could also rubber-stamp the number onto each pocket with an ink pad meant for fabric or write the numbers on with a fabric marker.

To add some color and make use of fabric you might already have laying around, Mmoody Kids founder Justine Bronaugh suggests using a mix of felt and patterned fabric scraps, like what she uses to make her signature patchwork pants. “Felt is a classic Christmas material that you can get at any craft store,” she says, adding that it is easy to cut and works well with hot glue for anyone who doesn’t want to or doesn’t have time to sew.

You can get felt by the yard at most craft stores, or you can order it online. Just make sure you know the measurements you need and check the width of the fabric you’re buying, as it can vary. Cut a big rectangle from the felt and then, Bronaugh suggests, cut pockets out of scrap fabric and use a contrasting color of felt for the numbers. You could also personalize the calendar with a name or initials cut out of felt. “If you wanted to really get crazy with it, you could make it in the shape of a Christmas tree or a star or something like that,” she says. Attach all the pockets and numbers to the backing with hot glue.

You could also buy a bunch of wavy Ric Rac trim and glue that on as embellishment or a border. Or if you know a crafty tween or teen you could ask them to help decorate the calendar with any kind of festive trims they like. Bronaugh recommends sourcing everything from your nearest local craft store or resale shop. “We have an amazing craft resale shop here that I go to all the time. A lot of cities have them; people just donate supplies and you can go in and get inspired by whatever you find,” she says.

Stevie Remsberg, New York senior visuals director, inherited a needlepoint Advent calendar made by her aunt that she has used year after year with her daughters, who are both teens now. Instead of pockets, it has small rings sewn onto it where you can tie 24 small bags to fill with gifts. She says you could do the same thing with any decorative textile you like. You’ll just need wooden or plastic craft rings and embroidery thread to attach them.

For the bags, Remsberg bought a bulk pack of muslin ones and simply wrote numbers (and her kids’ initials) on each one.

I like the idea of adding rings and gift bags to a Christmas-themed baby blanket or quilt.

But you could simply pin them on a thrifted kid’s quilt too.

Remsberg told me she recently saw a horizontal Advent calendar that used the same kind of drawstring bags but situated along a single wooden rod with the bags hanging off it on ribbons. “That would be so much easier than me tying all of my bags onto these little rings,” she says.

To hang it, you could even use a nice-looking straight stick you find outside.

Or an even simpler route would be to clip 24 large paper envelopes on a string with clothespins and tuck your goodies into the open envelope, as Boyle’s sister does each year.

If you are in a time crunch, there are plenty of blank Advent calendars available to buy that you can reuse year after year. In fact, almost anything can be an Advent calendar if it can hold, hang, or display 24 or 25 little surprises.

Your first option for filler is almost nothing at all. Both Boyle and designer Sarah Jean Culbreth recommend making Advent calendars that are primarily about the countdown to Christmas rather than gift-getting. This is especially easy to do with very young kids and sets a tone of what to expect each year.

Boyle suggests trying this with a simple canvas pocket calendar by adding a small doll or figurine like a baby Maileg mouse that kids get to move from pocket to pocket as they count down the days. Or you can make your own: “One year, when each of the kids wanted to be the one to move the calendar forward, I cut out three cardboard snowmen and stuck each on a bamboo skewer so they could each have their own marker to move,” Boyle says.

Culbreth is making a slightly different countdown Advent calendar this year based off one that her mother-in-law made years ago. The calendar has a Christmas tree above 25 pockets, each of which holds a different mini-ornament. Each morning, you pull out that day’s ornament and tie it onto one of 25 corresponding spaces on the tree. By the time you get to Christmas, the tree is fully decorated.

You could also involve older kids in this process and make a similar type of countdown calendar using cardboard and construction paper instead of fabric. Going the construction-paper route gives kids lots of opportunities for creative cutouts, and the whole thing will be very lightweight to hang.

Remsberg told me that one year the theme of her Advent calendar was slime. Each day held a different little tub of slime plus a bag of glitter or confetti or other mix-ins. It was a huge success with her kids, who were 8 and 10 at the time. “We had a slime laboratory constantly going in our house for a month, which was gross, but they were very pleased,” she says.

Experience gifts are perfectly suited to Advent calendars since they encourage spending time together as a family. According to Brittanyanne Jaramillo, who makes one Advent calendar for her five kids each year, they don’t have to be major blowout events. She recommends writing different cozy activities on cards — “Christmas movie night,” for example, or “Drive around to see Christmas lights” — and mixing them in with little trinkets and candy.

You can also add what Bronaugh calls “missions” for kids to accomplish in order to win a small prize. Her 5-year-old loves crafts and little games or scavenger hunts. So she recommends filling an Advent calendar with craft prompts plus the supplies needed to accomplish them, like making an ornament out of cardboard and gem stickers, or drawing a holiday family portrait with some paper and markers. She also recommends including a small tub of PlayDoh and a cookie cutter one day, for more open-ended sensory fun.

Now that her daughters are older, Remsberg has started adding skin care to their Advent calendar in place of slime. “Last year, I got a skin-care Advent calendar from Trader Joe’s that had lip balm, a mask, and a bunch of other things, so I split it up and repackaged it. I’ve found that you can actually save money by buying gift sets or other Advent calendars, even if they’re not 24 days, and break them down for parts that you then put in your DIY Advent calendar at home. This would also work well with beauty gift sets of lip balm, hand cream, hand sanitizer, and perfume. And you could supplement the rest of the 24 days with candy, trinkets, and activities.

“Because December is long and dark, I personally like to lean into the sweet-treat tradition of Advent calendars,” says Boyle who stocks up on treats like gelt, seasonal gummies, pirouette cookies, chocolate mint cremes, and mini-marshmallows at Trader Joe’s. “Every evening, I’d just stick a different trio of treats into a pocket. People always ask me this, but I absolutely do not preload the calendar with chocolate at the beginning of the month,” she explains, adding that she’d much rather give her kids a small piece of chocolate or candy every evening for the month of December than try to source 24 tiny trinkets for each of them.

entry.title: New Stuff Alert: A $3,500 Misen Set?
entry.summary: And a Buck Mason puffer that every menswear guy will want.
entry.content:
For this week’s Don’t Dillydally, we’ve rounded up a range of newly released products we’re particularly excited about, including a nice and neutral-looking mini space heater, stylish new stowable backpacks and duffel bags from Monos, and a massive Misen cookware set that costs more than $3,500.

Lest you get too cold in your Salter House nightgown this winter, everybody’s favorite cottagecore brand has come out with this cozy (yet cool-looking) merino sweater in collaboration with knitwear designer Camille Zacky. At nearly $500, it’s the kind of thing you may very well want to keep under lock and key when not in use, which is perhaps what the iconography is gesturing toward.

Our best overall travel pillow now provides an additional in-flight activity: coloring in some cute floral designs using the included markers. An excellent gift idea for any creatively inclined frequent fliers you know.

Speaking of travel, luggage brand Monos just launched a collection of packable backpacks and duffels that caused me to look twice. Lots of travel brands make similar packable day bags that scrunch down small, but few of them (in fact, probably none of them?) look as elegant as these ones. Another good gift idea.

All the cool runners I know are obsessed with Bandit. The brand’s entire winter collection just dropped, ready to help them achieve chilly morning and evening personal bests. (I’ll be in bed.)

Our menswear expert Michael Zhao assures me that these boots are a big deal among the more stylish members of the Buy It for Life community. They’re designed in collaboration with Gauthier Borsarello, the founder of French fashion magazine L’Étiquette, and look very spiffy sitting atop that Beastie Boys book in the photo.

Those boots likely won’t fit me, but I really want this down jacket that Sierra Designs has come out with for Buck Mason and could probably get away with a size small. It looks vintage but is actually brand new and comes in three tasteful colors.

Misen is crazy for this one. The DTC kitchen brand (that makes a lot of stuff we really like) is selling its entire collection in a bundle that promises to “help you figure out your credit-card limit.” In fairness, the stainless steel pots and pans in particular should last for decades if you treat them right. Maybe this is actually a bargain?

Cool moms and their children have probably already clicked on these new patchwork kids from Mmoody Kids. Yet another item of clothing on this list that tragically won’t fit me.

Windmill makes the quietest space heater that I’ve ever tested, and while the original size isn’t actually that cumbersome, I’m pretty excited about this new smaller version. It’d slide right under your desk during a cozy work-from-home day but is actually nice-enough looking to leave out for everybody to see.

entry.title: The 11 Very Best Bluetooth Speakers
entry.summary: For listening to music just about anywhere.
entry.content:
Bluetooth speakers have been a major fixture in my life ever since I picked up the original Ultimate Ears Boom in college. I use them to listen to podcasts or my favorite playlists while I’m cooking and cleaning my house, and if I’m going on a trip, I’ll take a travel-size speaker to make sure I’ve got my shower tunes.

To find the best Bluetooth speakers for listening at home, traveling, or multi-room audio, I tested 27 speakers from the biggest names in the space, including Ultimate Ears, JBL, Sonos, and Bose, and used each one for at least eight hours while listening to music in a variety of genres throughout my home.

Updated on November 24, 2026
I’ve added the JBL Pulse 6 as the new best Bluetooth speaker with LED lights. The rest of these Bluetooth speakers are still our favorites, and they’re all still available.

The speaker’s weight will help determine how easy it is to carry around and varies widely: Many models come in under one pound, but some can weigh more than ten pounds. Rugged speakers meant for outdoors tend to weigh more, louder speakers need bigger (and heavier) amplification circuitry and drivers, and smaller home-office speakers with less robust builds weigh less, though the smaller size and lighter build can mean in a slight drop in sound quality since more rigid construction can mean better performance.

I’ve found that the ideal weight for a speaker you will actually want to carry with you is about one pound: That’s big enough to project a good sound in a variety of spaces, small enough to throw into a bag for a trip, and light enough you won’t regret packing it. If you’re not planning on moving the speaker or don’t mind hauling around the extra weight, bigger speakers may be worth the trade-off for better sound. For larger speakers, I focused on those with some sort of handle to ensure they’re not cumbersome to move.

Most Bluetooth speakers have an IP rating, which tells you how protected the device is against water and dust. The first number indicates dust resistance, and the second tells you how waterproof the speaker is — in both cases, the higher the number, the better the protection. But if you’re going to use your speaker near any water — like in the shower or near a pool — you should get one with a waterproof rating of at least 7 for protection against submersion.

Every speaker on this list can clock at least seven hours with decent recharge times. Naturally, larger speakers will have larger batteries, but even small speakers should offer over six hours of battery life.

Some manufacturers make Bluetooth speakers that also have built-in voice assistants (either Alexa or Google Assistant, or both).

Weight: 0.93 pounds | Dust and water resistance: IP67 | Battery life: 14 hours| Smart assistant: No

Among all the speakers I’ve tested, none have impressed me quite as much as the Wonderboom 4, mainly owing to the quality of sound it’s able to produce in such a small package. It’s about the size of a small candle and can easily fit into a backpack, carry-on, or even a tote, yet it’s loud enough to hear from across my living room, all the way into my kitchen.

Pairing is simple: All you have to do is hold the pairing button and it shows up in your phone or tablet’s Bluetooth menu right away. It will connect immediately when powered back on. You can easily pair two Wonderbooms together for a stereo experience with a couple button pushes.

At louder levels, usually around 80 percent or higher, sounds can start to get muddled, especially with genres like hip-hop or metal (I tested with Lil Wayne’s Tha Carter II and Lamb of God’s Sacrament), and the vocals can drown out instrumentals. It’s not enough to detract from how good the Wonderboom sounds, though. When kept below that threshold, songs sound as clear and vibrant as on other UE speakers such as the Boom. As for podcasts and audiobooks, I was able to play those at louder volumes without audio quality suffering, and could hear them over the water running as I washed my dishes.

The Wonderboom 4 is chunkier than the JBL Clip 5, so it’s slightly less portable, and its elastic loop is less effective than the Clip 5’s metal clasp for attaching it to things, but the speaker also produces clearer sound, likely owing to its larger size.

To test its IP67 rating, I dropped the Wonderboom into a pool of water in my sink three times while playing music. The music sounded muffled and quite terrible at first, but once the water dripped out, the speaker was back to sounding good as new. You absolutely should not try this, but know that if you’re using this as your pool-party speaker, it’s safe. It has a plastic door that covers the charging port when not in use to prevent water from sneaking in and mucking things up. It’s rugged enough to withstand being carried with you on your next vacation, or just getting moved from room to room.

While the Clip 5 and Go 4 are both smaller than the Wonderboom 4, this is the most portable speaker I’ve tested that gets closest to the sound quality of bigger speakers like the Pulse 6. It’s quite similar to our previous best Bluetooth speaker overall, the Wonderboom 3: Its sound is nearly identical, and the design hasn’t changed. The biggest improvement is the switch from micro-USB to USB-C, which will make the Wonderboom 4 easier to travel with if you have a phone or laptop that charges over USB-C (as most do these days). For this model, Ultimate Ears also added a podcast mode to the equalizer, and while it did make voices sound more crisp, I didn’t find the difference noticeable enough to change modes when listening to audiobooks or podcasts.

Weight: 0.56 pounds | Dust and water resistance: IP67 | Battery life: 16 hours| Smart assistant: No

If you want to get a speaker that’s affordable and doesn’t cut corners on audio quality, Sony’s SRS XB100 sounds surprisingly good for costing well under $100. The sound isn’t quite as clear at loud volumes as with the Wonderboom, but the Sony has louder bass, which some people may prefer. While listening to Elton John’s Madman Across the Water, I found the vocals easy to hear without the instrumentals being washed out. For hip-hop tracks like Run the Jewels’ Blockbuster Night Pt. 1, the bass felt punchy without overpowering Killer Mike or El-P’s vocals, even with the volume turned up while I was running a robot vacuum in another room.

While JBL and Logitech use a fabric covering over their speakers, Sony uses a matte plastic finish that’s more durable, easy to grip, and pleasant to look at (the speaker comes in four colors, including vibrant shades of orange and blue). The speaker has a fabric loop that you can easily attach to a backpack (though the Clip 5’s mechanism is more effective). It also has the longest battery life of any travel-size speaker I’ve tested, lasting about 13 hours.

Weight: 0.62 pounds | Dust and water resistance: IP67 | Battery life: 12 hours| Smart assistant: No

Most of these Bluetooth speakers are portable, but the Clip 5 is the most travel-friendly I’ve tested thanks to the built-in eponymous clip that lets you attach it to nearly anything, including a bike basket or showerhead. The speaker has rubber ribs on the back that allow you to place it on smooth surfaces without having to worry about it sliding all over the place — helpful since it can’t stand upright like the other speakers I’ve tested. The speaker is waterproof and dustproof, and it can withstand a few knocks against a hard surface.

It’s easy to underestimate the sound quality of a speaker as small as the Clip 5. In my testing, it managed to sound clear and vibrant even with outdoor sounds like waves and wind in the background. In the shower, podcasts were easy to hear over the water, and I never had to blast it to full volume just to catch what someone said. Over a couple weeks of testing, I was able to get about 12 hours of battery life out of the Clip 5. If you mostly use this in the shower or when you’re traveling, you can easily go a month between charges.

My only gripe with the Clip 5 is that, unlike the Clip 4, the buttons for turning the device on and off and pairing to other devices aren’t raised buttons. That makes them harder to operate if you can’t see them, like when the speaker is clipped behind a showerhead. The buttons for play/pause and volume are all raised and are on the front of the speaker so they’re easy to see and access, but I wish that were true of all the buttons.

Weight: 6.61 pounds | Dust and water resistance: IP56 | Battery life: 24 hours | Smart assistant: Yes

Many speakers I’ve tested can be connected to other speakers for a richer sound experience, but Sonos still does it best. The Move 2 is significantly larger than the Wonderboom, so you probably won’t want to take it with you on your weekend getaway, but it’s still small enough to carry from room to room, and the built-in handle lets you do so easily. I’m also impressed that, unlike nearly every other speaker I’ve tested, the Move 2 has a removable battery, which should make it straightforward to replace. To do so on most other speakers, you’d have to buy a third-party kit and do it yourself.

While the Move 2 is pricier than similar-size speakers like the JBL Pulse 6, its sound is nearly unmatched. The bass is loud and powerful (though not as heavy as the Brane X), vocals sound crisp, and everything sounds clear even at full volume.

The Move 2 has all of Sonos’s smart features, like multi-speaker pairing and adaptive audio (altering the sound to fit your room), and can easily be controlled and adjusted from within the Sonos app. It also has direct Amazon Alexa integration, so you can use it as your main smart speaker, and AirPlay integration that lets you stream directly from your Apple Devices without having to pair over Bluetooth.

Given its name, it’s no surprise that the Move 2 is so easy to lug around, but its charging method isn’t quite as mobile. Instead of using a simple charging cable like most companies, Sonos gave the Move 2 a docking station, which is basically a ring that you plop the bottom of the speaker into when it needs to charge.

With an IP rating of IP56, it’s not as protected from the elements as the Pulse or the Brane, but it’s still protected from heavy jets of water, so it should be safe from some raindrops (but not from a drop in the pool).

Weight: 10.8 pounds | Dust and water resistance: No IP rating | Battery: 8 hours | Smart assistant: Yes

For those who talk to their speakers as much as they listen, JBL’s Authentics 300 speaker balances functionality, good looks, and quality sound in a relatively portable design. It’s bigger than every other speaker we recommend but that also gives it louder sound, and the included handle makes it easy to tote around the house (but note that it weighs nearly 11 pounds). That handle is easier to grip than the one on the Move 2, though given the Authentics’s larger size, the Move 2 is easier to take with you when you leave the house. If you do want to travel with the Authentics 300, it’s small enough to store behind the passenger seat.

Of the speakers I’ve tested, this one’s classy ’70s style makes the Authentics 300 one of my favorites to display. The front of the speaker is covered in a patterned fabric that’s reminiscent of JBL’s classic L100 bookshelf speaker, and the top has three large knobs you can turn to control the volume, as well as the speaker’s treble and bass levels. Each knob has an LED that wraps around the dial and lights up to indicate the current levels for each toggle. The controls on the 300 are more fun to play with than the clicky buttons of the Wonderboom 4 and Clip 5, but I prefer the dials on the Teenage Engineering OB-4 of all the speaker controls I’ve tried.

Sound on the Authentics 300 is loud and impressive: While blasting music at 80 percent volume from my living room, I could hear it from across my three-bedroom home, and in some cases, podcasts were discernible as well. Given its size, it makes sense that the speaker is louder than the Move 2 or Pulse 6, but I’ve been impressed with how clear the sound remains, even at high volumes.

The speaker’s defining feature is its ability to connect to both Google Assistant and Alexa. I’ve found that Alexa is better for controlling smart home gear like light bulbs and robot vacuums, but I prefer Google Assistant for asking general questions and getting info about the weather. While alternating between the assistants in succession, responses were as quick as they are with a dedicated smart speaker like the Echo Dot or Nest Hub. The Authentics also has an ethernet port if you want to make sure it has a reliable internet connection. On the other hand, if you want to disable this speaker’s smart features altogether, there’s a switch to turn off the microphone on the back, which is not something many speakers with microphones offer.

Unfortunately, unlike most speakers we recommend, the Authentics 300 doesn’t have any official IP rating, so I wouldn’t recommend bringing this speaker anywhere it might get wet. For outdoor use, you should get the Brane X, depending on how large your gathering is.

Weight: 7.7 pounds | Dust and water resistance: IP57 | Battery: 12 hours| Smart assistant: Yes

For those who prefer to control their music over Spotify Connect instead of Bluetooth, the Brane X strikes a nice balance between connectivity and portability. It has traditional Bluetooth pairing for when you’re on the go, but if it’s connected to Wi-Fi, you and others connected to your network can cast songs to it using Spotify or AirPlay. It also sounds incredible.

Despite being relatively portable, the Brane is one of the loudest, bassiest speakers I’ve ever tested. That doesn’t seem possible, given that the Brane is so portable, but Brane has managed to pack a party’s worth of bass into a speaker that won’t take up much room on your desk. Its mids and treble sounded just as good, even with the volume cranked all the way up.

Just like the JBL Authentics 300, this speaker has built-in Alexa integration so you can control your music and smart-home gear hands-free. It also works with Spotify Connect and Pandora, as well as a few other music services. Of the bunch, Spotify Connect is the most useful. As long as the Brane is connected to a Wi-Fi network, anyone with a Spotify account who’s connected to the same network can cast music right to this speaker without needing to log in to their account in the speaker’s accompanying app.

While this speaker is quite impressive, I have some complaints. Unlike nearly every other speaker I’ve tested, this one has an annoyingly bulky charger. It comes in two parts, one of which has a large brick that’s heavy and inconspicuous. I’m also not a fan of the built-in handle. It works, but it’s made of a rubbery material that wraps around the edge of the speaker a bit too tightly, making it hard to pull off and grab the speaker. Finally, I wish the buttons on the top were illuminated, as is the case with other speakers that cost this much.

Weight: 3.2 pounds | Dust and water resistance: IP68 | Battery: 12 hours | Smart assistant: No

JBL’s Pulse 6 is one of the best-looking speakers I’ve ever tested. Its lava lamp-like design makes listening sessions feel like a personal concert, and its new light-up handle adds both utility and flair. Beyond that, its sound is loud and clear enough to fill a room.

Where most party speakers (including the ULT Field 5 below) use LED lights as accents, the entire body of the Pulse is made up of them. The speaker is wrapped in a clear casing that lets the lights of the Pulse glow through. There are 16 total lighting presets, all of which are stunning to look at while listening to music. There’s the “cheers” mode, which makes the whole speaker look like a fizzy mug of beer; the “campfire” setting for a more rustic vibe; and the “sea” mode if you fancy a sea shanty.

If you want to use the Pulse as a light without music playing, there’s a mode for that, too. When in “bedside” mode, you don’t get as much control over the color of the light — you can adjust from amber to a gentle white — but there’s enough customizability to get the lighting in your bedroom just right. It’s nowhere near as harsh as an overhead light and feels more like the lighting you’d get out of something like the Loftie Lamp.

The Pulse’s light-show capabilities are certainly the main attraction, but the speaker sounds great, too. The bass has plenty of oomph for personal listening (though I’d recommend the Field 5 for parties), and songs come through with crisp detail. There’s also Auracast built in, meaning you can group multiple Pulses together in a Sonos-like fashion. And if you want lossless audio, all you need to do is plug your playback device into the Pulse 6 using a USB-C cable.

Weight: 7.27 pounds | Dust and water resistance: IP67 | Battery: 25 hours| Smart assistant: No

Although the Pulse 6 is an excellent piece of eye candy, I recommend Sony’s ULT Field 5 for indoor parties. It has richer bass and gets louder than the Pulse 6, while being easier to move around thanks to an included shoulder strap.

While this speaker is louder and has heavier bass than the Pulse 6, its lighting setup isn’t as robust or eye-catching. Rather than having lights that cover the entire surface of the speaker, the Field 5 has two rings of lights on the sides of the speaker, as well as lights inside the ULT logo on the top. The speaker doesn’t get as bright as the Pulse, but it still syncs the lights to whatever you’re playing.

Weight: 9.25 pounds | Dust and water resistance: Not listed | Battery: N/A | Smart assistant: No

If you want a speaker that can pair with your phone over Bluetooth or connect to all the other audio gear in your home without going all in on Sonos, get Audio Pro’s C10 MKII, which works with gear from the home audio brand WiiM. While Sonos is the most popular brand in multiroom audio, WiiM is a platform-agnostic, audiophile-friendly alternative that works with traditional audio equipment like bookshelf speakers and amps. Just like Sonos, it has integration with Spotify, Tidal, and some more obscure services like Roon and Qobuz. Typically, you need one of WiiM’s devices — which don’t have speakers of their own — to get started, but the C10 MKII has WiiM’s software built in, and you can tie it to all your other WiiM gear.

The C10 MKII is slightly narrower than the Authentics 300, but its sound is even clearer and more balanced at loud volumes, and it has less prominent bass than the Brane X. In addition to controls for volume and playback, there are six preset buttons that you can use to create shortcuts for your favorite music on Spotify and buttons for casting audio to different devices. Because this speaker is meant to tie into other home-audio gear, it also has inputs for connecting to a record player, as well as an output for hooking it up to a subwoofer.

Unlike every other Bluetooth speaker on this list, the C10 MKII doesn’t have a battery, so it works only when plugged into an outlet. That makes it less portable, but because it’s the only speaker that officially works with WiiM’s platform, and because it can work with so many other pieces of stereo equipment, it’s the most customizable speaker we recommend. If you want something that sounds almost as good but has more portability, get the JBL Authentics 300.

Weight: 3.74 pounds | Dust and water resistance: Not listed | Battery: 72 hours | Smart assistant: No

In addition to its top-notch sound, no speaker I’ve tested looks nearly as good as the OB-4 — which has an old-fashioned minimalist boom-box styling — from Swedish electronics company Teenage Engineering. While playing film soundtracks, hip-hop, and classic rock, the sound quality remained consistently vibrant.

For anyone who likes to be more hands-on with their listening, the OB-4 also has more playback and recording functions than any other speaker that I’ve tried. You can pair it to your phone over Bluetooth, or use it as an FM radio. You can also use its line-in input for analogue playback with devices like an old iPod or an instrument, and it has a looping function that lets you remix tracks right on the device using a rotating disc. That disc can also be used to manually rewind and fast-forward tracks, which I found myself fiddling with constantly. When you’re spinning it, the speaker plays a delightful sound that makes it feel like you’re rewinding a tape. Its other on-device controls for volume and pairing are reminiscent of old-school audio gear, and it’s fun to play around with both.

The handle, though thin, is strong and secure, so you don’t have to worry about dropping the speaker as you lug it around. You can fold the handle toward the back of the speaker to turn it into a stand, though I haven’t found that to be particularly useful.

It’s as much a decorative statement as it is a music device, and it’s quite gorgeous. When I had it sitting on my shelf, I received multiple compliments on it. It loses some of its wow factor once you look at its price tag, but if you’re a design-loving music nerd, this speaker checks every box.

JBL Go 4: The Go 4 is smaller than the Clip 5, but it doesn’t have a way to latch onto anything substantial on its own. It has a fabric loop, but you’ll still need a carabiner or other clip to attach it to a bag. It’s a fine speaker, but Sony’s XB100 is cheaper, and the Clip 5 sounds better and has more portability for just a bit more money.

entry.title: The Best Holiday Gifts for Every Type of Sister
entry.summary: Whether she’s a Pilates princess or a serious home chef.
entry.content:
I come from a long line of sisters. My grandmother was one of four, my mom is one of three, and I have two myself. So I’ll be the first to admit that depending on the day, they’re a built-in best friend — or, sometimes, a little bit of a nuisance. Still, when you’ve known someone from newborns to gray hairs, the gifting pressure is high. You’ll want to avoid one of the many gifts you’ve already given her, but you also want to surprise her with something that shows how much she means to you. I suggest using that lifetime of shared stories and experiences to your advantage: Gifts that are usually off-limits for colleagues and acquaintances — think, a phone case she’ll need to use everyday or a gadget that reminds her of her wrinkles — can actually show your sister how well you know her (and how much you love her). To help you find a gift that’s right for your sister, I dug through our archives and pulled some recommendations that succeeded within my own lineage. And if you’re looking for more gift inspiration, here’s every gift guide from the Strategist this year — which includes gifts for wives, mothers-in-law, college students, and other hard-to-shop-for types.

Tortoiseshell has become something of an elegant neutral. Many iterations of the pattern lean too khaki-colored, too splotchy, or too crackled for my taste, but I think this phone case gets it just right.

Strategist writer Brenley Goertzen and I both get a little sad when our Pointe Studio grip socks are dirty. The patterns make them a step up from your average Pilates socks, and they don’t lose their grip over time.

This book was described to me as “Love Island in a dystopian world.” I pored through it in two days and am planning to give a copy to my sister this Christmas.

They’ll be the centerpiece of the cheese-and-crackers spread at her next mahjong competition.

The latest micro-trend, according to our friends at The Cut, are foot undies, otherwise known as “lace socks peek-a-boo-ing out of a shoe.” These ones from Etsy are a nice option (that you could pair with a new pair of flats if you’re feeling generous).

When I tried all of Abercrombie’s tees earlier this year, this was my favorite. It’s slouchy without being zhlubby thanks in part to a thicker neckline, and it can be dressed up or down.

The 100 percent cotton laptop case is made of dark-wash denim to match her vintage 501’s.

What better way to protect her bombshell blowout than with a Victoria’s Secret umbrella in the company’s signature stripe?

This stretchy neoprene belt can fit your sister’s phone and keys. Goertzen owns one and appreciates how comfortable it is to wear.

When former Strategist senior editor and chef Kiki Aranita tested this hot-pot starter set, she found it allowed for a seamless at-home hot-pot experience. She used it to warm up parboiled potatoes straight from the refrigerator, too.

The order deadline for Abbode’s custom Instagrammable waffle pouches is fast approaching, but this one is premade and available for (free) two-day shipping.

These design-y hand weights aren’t all looks: Goertzen says they’re easier to hold with a neutral grip, so she’s never putting strain on her wrists.

Hugz’s stuffed animals merge the best parts of a weighted blanket and a heating pad. You can throw this adorable Highland cow (or a hammerhead shark or a spotted giraffe) in the freezer or the microwave depending on your temperature needs.

Vacuum steamers are the latest breakthrough in garment-steaming technology. When Strategist writer Erin Schwartz tested each one in the new category, they preferred this one, which, they say, “got a shirt so crisp you could crack an egg on it.”

Consider the Solawave an intro to red-light therapy. It’s ideal for quick spot treatments or smaller areas like the lip-line or under eyes.

Coach is on a revival tour. The company’s leather Teri bag is topping teen wish lists, and its bags made of leftover and recycled materials sell out quickly on Depop. These shearling-lined clogs are a nice option for the sister who’s already toting around a Brooklyn shoulder bag.

When we stopped people on the street to ask about their work bags, we found this one three times. It has pockets on the inside and outside, so she has a spot for all her glosses and valuables.

So long as she has the space, this is the next best thing to a standing massage appointment. The at-home massage table has three types of rollers that can relax muscles, target deep-set tension, and mimic a deep tissue massage, respectively.

ICYMI: Pink outdoor gear is everywhere right now. If she already has salmon-colored Salomons and a raspberry-colored raincoat, you may as well get her a pink tent to match.

entry.title: Get the Pet Parent in Your Life a Customized Gift
entry.summary: Including sculptures, an embroidered bag, and a painting from Fishs Eddy’s in-house pet-portrait artist.
entry.content:
I’ve been a dogsitter for a long time, so I’ve become well-acquainted with some truly obsessed pet parents. And while it may seem “first thought,” these people really do just want gifts about their fur babies. The more specific, the better. But I’ve seen a lot of truly terrible personalized pet gifts over the years — the nearly $300 “Cuddle Clone” I helped a bereaved dog mom design still haunts my dreams, not to mention all the ugly pillow pets and horrible AI Etsy portraits — so below, a selection of more tasteful custom pet gifts. Note that since the holidays are in full swing, and ordering deadlines are changing by the day, you should triple-check before making a purchase.

Staud partners with Los Angeles–based custom embroidering company C.Bonz to make these soft jersey sweatshirts, which can be adorned with up to two pet faces.

Staud is also more generally known for its bags, and its Kaia purse can be hand-painted with your four-legged friend. Like the sweatshirt above, you can choose up to two pets, but the artist can paint the entire body. Plus any accessories your pet may love, including clothing or a favorite toy, can also be included in the portrait.

If you prefer a larger daily schlepper, Mark & Graham has this sturdy cotton canvas tote. You can choose between five popular breeds — chocolate lab, yellow lab, Frenchie, goldendoodle, and terrier — and then customize it with your pooch’s name or monogram, for free.

Or customize the pocketbooks you already own with a hand-painted bag charm.

Popular embroidering brand Abbode offers both “Dog Mom” and “Cat Mom” waffle weave pouches. You can choose one dog or cat icon — they have over 90 breeds to choose from — and then customize with a saying of your choice. In addition to the olive color shown, the pouches are available in 11 other options.

Ben Lenovtiz is the in-house pet-portrait artist at Fishs Eddy who has painted thousands of New York’s beloved animals over the years. This holiday season he has opened up 50 commissions, which are guaranteed to ship by Christmas if you order by November 30. For procrastinators, after that date, there is a $150 rush fee, with an absolute final ordering day of December 11.

For a more affordable option, there are plenty of pet portraits available on Etsy. I’m particularly fond of this sweet watercolor. To make the gift complete, frame it before wrapping.

Artist Janie Korn’s candle sculptures have been featured everywhere (the Cut commissioned her in 2020 to cast that season’s best runway looks in wax). For just $150, a true steal for a Korn original, she will make a four-inch candle of your pet.

If you prefer a figurine in a less ephemeral medium, Slop Ceramics offers hand-sculpts and hand-paints each of these. The artist requests at least four photos of your furry friend and that extra attention to their personalities and individual markings really shine through in their playful pieces. They are available in both small, which measures roughly two to three inches, and large, which measures between six and seven inches.

While you could customize an ornament with a picture of your pet, these handfelted two-inch figures are even better, since they’re basically mini sculptures that hang on your tree.

A one-of-a-kind ceramic mug, available in ten glazes, for the pet parent who likes to start the day with some couch cuddles and a cup of coffee.

Sure, you could raid your grandmother’s jewelry box for a brooch. Or, for just $80, this Etsy artists will hand-bead a brooch of your pet. (Also available as a keychain or ornament.)

Socks can make a great gift when they are especially nice. A pair of socks with their dog embroidered on them? Perhaps the nicest of all.

entry.title: 84 Delightful, Surprising, Actually Useful White-Elephant Gifts
entry.summary: A compendium of presents that everyone at the party will want to steal.
entry.content:
White-elephant gift exchanges — in which everyone brings a secret gift and takes turns selecting (or stealing) a gift — are among my favorite holiday traditions. However, they usually lean toward gag gifts, and I cannot stand the wastefulness of buying something no one will actually want to take home just for laughs. So I propose bringing something delightful, surprising, and downright useful to your next white-elephant gathering. The best white-elephant gifts are items that anyone in your group could enjoy — a helpful doodad, a tasty treat, or an unusual version of an everyday essential. Below, I’ve compiled my best ideas for non-junky, truly special white-elephant gifts that people will surely want to steal. And since most of these gift exchanges have a specific budget, I’ve sorted my recommendations by price.

Editor’s note: Since many items on this list are on sale for Black Friday, I’ve listed them by their sale price, not the full price.

A Sunprint Kit is a fun throwback activity that’ll actually encourage the recipient to spend some time outside this winter.

Give the gift of eliminating anxiety over getting hit with overweight baggage fees at the airport.

This citrus lip balm that writer Bella Druckman found at a gift shop in Maine is like a more grown-up version of the Eos sphere lip balms.

A pair of giant tweezers is a surprisingly useful kitchen tool that most people likely don’t already have.

Washing up after a big family dinner will be much cheerier with a sparkly disco sponge.

This mix of garlic, Calabrian chile, parsley, and sea salt is perfect for sprinkling into spaghetti (or any other dish, really). It’s the Strega Nona version of pixie dust.

BeanBoozled is about as close to a gag gift as I’ll recommend since it’s a game and ultimately is consumable. Playing with mixed-age groups that include kids is especially entertaining: Spin the wheel to determine which Jelly Belly color you’ll taste — it may be a friendly favorite like peach or a truly nasty one like barf.

Equal parts adorable and handy.

These charming reusable hand warmers will put a smile on their face even if the weather is freezing cold.

A big ol’ raviolo makes a pleasant pillow for a spoon.

Writer Tembe Denton-Hurst says playing Murdle logic games has stopped her from doomscrolling — something we could all stand to have some help with.

These dachshund-shaped under-eye patches are trending among teens, but I think they are fun for all ages.

Keep their fridge smelling fresh, no matter how many Thanksgiving or Christmas leftovers end up in there.

Everyone needs to degunk their tech periodically. Make that chore easier with this mini cleaning kit.

The absolutely “essential” German lip balm recommended by actress Lauren Ambrose will work for just about anyone once the winter dryness sets in.

A slightly elevated — and yet more whimsical — version of the koozie.

A lighter shaped like a matchstick is exactly the right mix of offbeat and actually useful — the length makes lighting candles easier than it is with a simple BIC.

Here’s a plant they can’t kill — plus an indoor activity for a bleak winter day.

Eat an NYC slice, no matter where you actually live: This kit includes all the ingredients needed to make a pizza at home, plus a bottle of unfiltered NYC tap water for authenticity.

No more rummaging around in a Dopp kit: This organizer used by professional makeup artists is also nice for traveling or keeping products for touch-ups in a purse.

A more elegant way to prop up their phone when cooking, reading, or playing music.

Flossing is a lot more fun with flavors like cherry, vanilla, and confetti cake.

Preempt the mess with these optical-illusion coasters that resemble real drink spills.

Don’t worry, they’re unscented.

Everyone could use a protective and stylish glasses case. This one is made of stainless steel so the glasses inside will never get scratched or dented, plus it’s small enough to fit in a purse, says comedian Kate Berlant.

Forget the seasonal scented candle and bring seasonal scented laundry detergent. This one smells like cinnamon, nutmeg, smoked marshmallow, peppered gingerbread, vetiver, and milky musks.

For the multi-beverage lifestyle.

Ana Gasteyer told us this old-fashioned popcorn-maker is one of the best gifts she’s ever received. Pair it with some fancy kernels or seasonings for maximum effect.

This teeny Kodak on a keychain actually works as a digital camera that can take photo and video. It’s also a blind box, so which camera design is inside will be a surprise to you and your gift recipient.

An umbrella is always good to have on hand, and this one with a raining-cats-and-dogs print will brighten even the gloomiest of rainy days.

This beeswax-wrapped bag keeps bread fresh for a whole week. I’d pair it with a loaf from my favorite local bakery.

A tiny water bottle makes for easy sipping on the go. This one will easily fit in their bag or clip on like a bag charm. Choose from a black cat, a brown bear, or a black-and-white cow character.

This sweet little hedgehog doubles as a doorstop and a brush for cleaning the bottom of shoes.

A silk sleep mask, beloved by Strategist staffers and celebrities alike, is a luxe upgrade almost anyone could appreciate.

They’ll be thinking of you every day when their coffee actually stays hot all morning in Ember’s self-heating mug. Senior editor Jen Trolio says the Ember is one of the best gifts she’s ever received.

An absolutely massive quantity of a normal product is a shortcut to a great white-elephant gift. Case in point: 64 ounces of pure Vermont maple syrup.

Multiple Strategist staffers (myself included) swear by this ergonomic mouse. Their hands and wrists will thank you.

Everyone needs one really good pair of scissors. These ones, according to actress Zosia Mamet, won’t “poop out on you.”

Kate McLeod’s foot-care set offers a luxe upgrade on a typical buff and lotion routine. The glass buffer–slash–callous remover is beautiful and easy to use, while the moisturizing foot stone softens the skin and smells fresh.

East Fork’s candles are poured in a reusable vessel, so once your giftee has burned through the candle, they are left with a beautiful piece of handmade pottery. The panettone scent is festive without being too on the nose.

Camp Snap’s screen-free video cameras mimic the old Super 8 cameras — a digital camera for the nostalgic era. Denton-Hurst says the camera gives an old home-video look that’s warm and vibey.

For schlepping with ease and style.
